claims.source: Run on pandas 3.0.6 and 3.0.2 in this repository (predict-output exercise).

concept_html:
A pure function returns a value that depends only on its arguments, and changes nothing outside itself: no file writes, no global variables, no mutation of the inputs, no printing, no clock or random calls it does not receive.

def weighted_mean(values: list[float], weights: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(v * w for v, w in zip(values, weights, strict=True)) / sum(weights)

Pure functions are easy to test (inputs in, answer out), safe to reuse, and safe to run twice. Most analysis logic can be pure: cleaning, feature building, statistics, scoring.

Some work is not pure by nature: reading files, calling APIs, writing tables, logging, reading the clock. Push that work to the edges of the program, into a thin layer that gathers inputs, calls the pure core, and writes results.

read (impure) -> transform, compute (pure) -> write (impure)

Three side effects hide easily in data code:

  • Mutating an argument. df["x"] = ... or rows.append(...) inside a function changes the caller's object. The caller did not ask for that. Return a new object instead: df.assign(x=...), or build a new list.
  • Reading globals. A function that reads a module-level THRESHOLD or TODAY gives different answers after someone changes it. Pass it in.
  • Hidden time and randomness. datetime.now() or np.random.rand() inside a function makes its output untestable. Pass a date, or a numpy.random.Generator.

In pandas 3, Copy-on-Write is always on, so many operations already return new objects. Assigning a column with df[col] = ... still changes df itself, which is exactly the mutation to keep out of shared functions.

lines: import pandas as pd
def score_respondents(df: pd.DataFrame, as_of_year: int, threshold: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Add age and high_reach. Returns a new frame; the input is unchanged."""
return df.assign(
age=as_of_year - df["birth_year"],
high_reach=df["reach"] > threshold,
)
def main(input_path: str, output_path: str, as_of_year: int, threshold: float) -> None:
"""The edge: read, call the pure core, write."""
scored = score_respondents(pd.read_csv(input_path), as_of_year, threshold)
scored.to_csv(output_path, index=False)

solution_lines: import pandas as pd
def add_age(df: pd.DataFrame, as_of_year: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Return a copy of df with age = as_of_year - birth_year."""
return df.assign(age=as_of_year - df["birth_year"])

title: Pure functions, side effects at the edges
why_html:
A feature function adds age_group to the DataFrame it receives, in place. The training script calls it, then passes the same DataFrame to a stratified split on age_group. Later, someone reorders the calls so the split runs first. The split fails with a KeyError on one laptop and works on another, depending on which notebook cells ran before.

A pure add_age_group(df) -> DataFrame that returns a new frame gives the same result in every order, and its test needs three rows.
